# ISSUE 5: COMPETING DEMANDS FOR AVAILABLE WATER AND STATUTORY HIERARCHY

## Issue

How does Ghanaian law prioritize competing demands for water when a licensed mining operation seeks to expand its abstraction, and existing downstream users (domestic consumers, public water utilities, farmers, and environmental flows) rely on the same watercourse? Specifically: (a) does the law establish an explicit statutory hierarchy among mining, domestic consumption, public water supply, agriculture, and environmental requirements; (b) what criteria and legal standards must the Water Resources Commission apply when deciding whether to grant, refuse, or condition a water permit for the expansion; (c) whether existing downstream users and environmental flows have protected legal status; and (d) how Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) principles inform the allocation decision?

---

## Rule

**Primary Law: Statutory Hierarchy of Water Uses**The Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 7 establishes that "In considering an application, the Commission shall be guided by (a) the prevailing water policy, (b) domestic water use, and (c) any other water use which fulfils the goals of national socio-economic development. Where the priorities of two applications are the same, the first in time shall be given the priority."[verbatim] This is the binding operative rule on priority allocation.

The hierarchy is explicit: **domestic water use is the primary guiding criterion**; socio-economic development uses (which may include mining and irrigation) are secondary; where two uses rank equally in tier, temporal priority (first application granted) determines allocation.

**Trust Duty and Public Interest**"The property in and control of all water resources is vested in the President on behalf of, and in trust for the people of Ghana" (Water Resources Commission Act, 1996 (Act 522), section 12).[verbatim] Water is held for collective benefit, not for exclusive exploitation by any sector.

**No Standalone Mining Entitlement to Water**The Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), section 17 provides that the holder of a mineral right must obtain "the requisite approvals or licenses from the Water Resources Commission before it may '…obtain, divert, impound, convey and use water from a river, stream, underground reservoir or watercourse within the land the subject of the mineral right'."[verbatim] A mineral right does not automatically confer entitlement to water; WRC approval is a mandatory separate gate.

**Permit Review Standard: Irreparable Harm and Basin-Wide Impact**The WRC must review applications "to ascertain that the proposed water use is in accordance with the national water use policies and plans and will not cause irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment," and must hold "a public hearing in cases where…the WRC considers that the proposed use will have a negative impact on the natural resources of a basin."[verbatim] Permits that meet this standard may be granted; those that do not may be refused or conditioned.

**Basin-Level Priority in Water Scarcity**Article 10 of the Water Charter for the Volta River Basin (December 2018) states: "Among all the different types of water use in the Basin, no particular use shall be given priority over the others. However, should competing uses of water prevent all the requirements from being met, special attention shall be paid to the basic needs of human beings."[verbatim] Where water is insufficient for all users, basic human needs—drinking water, sanitation, essential domestic use—prevail.

**Integration of Agencies: WRC Role in Mineral Permitting**The standing technical committee of the Minerals Commission includes a representative from the Water Resources Commission. When an application is submitted to the Minerals Commission, the WRC representative advises the committee as to the effect of the proposed mineral operations on water bodies in and around the mining area. If the proposed mining operation will adversely affect water resources for which there can be no appreciable remedial action to reduce or minimize the adverse effect, the Minerals Commission may advise the Minister to set the land aside as an ecologically fragile area. If the applicant must obtain a water use license, the WRC can indicate such requirement so that the grant of the mineral right by the Minister will be subject to a water use license obtained from the WRC.[verbatim]

This establishes a procedural safeguard: water impacts on the mineral operation are examined early, and irreversible harm to water resources can trigger land-use exclusion.

---

## Application

**The Statutory Priority Framework and Asempa Gold's Expansion**

Start with Regulation 7 of L.I. 1692. It divides water uses into two tiers:
- **Tier 1 (Primary):** Domestic water use.
- **Tier 2 (Secondary):** Uses fulfilling national socio-economic development goals.

The Adom River serves multiple Tier 1 uses:
1. Drinking water for downstream communities.
2. Domestic activities (washing, sanitation) for residents.
3. Public water supply to two district capitals via Ghana Water Company Ltd (Ghana Water).

These are not new aspirations or future plans. They are **established existing uses** with settled beneficiaries.

Asempa Gold's proposed expansion is a Tier 2 use: industrial mining for economic development and foreign exchange. Mining generates royalties, tax revenue, and employment—classic socio-economic development goals.

**The Temporal Priority Rule and Its Application**

Regulation 7(2) provides that where two applications rank equally in priority tier, "the first in time shall be given the priority."

The facts establish that:
- Downstream communities have used the Adom River for drinking and domestic purposes presumably for decades, if not generations.
- Ghana Water has been abstracting from the river approximately 35 km downstream for an unspecified period to supply two district capitals.
- Asempa Gold's mining commenced at an unspecified date, and the expansion is now proposed.

On temporal grounds alone, the established domestic and public utility uses have priority over the expansion. The expansion is not the first application; it is an incremental increase to an already licensed operation, competing with pre-existing established uses.

**The "Irreparable Damage" Standard and the Evidence**

Regulation 4 of L.I. 1692 requires the WRC to refuse or condition permits that cause "irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment."

Three forms of harm are now documented:

1. **Reduction in dry-season flows:**Mining operations have put stress on the quantity and quality of water in mining areas.Farmers downstream report that "the volume of water available during the dry season has declined considerably since mining commenced." If the expansion proceeds, further reduction is predictable. This directly affects Tier 1 uses (domestic consumption by downstream communities and irrigators).

2. **Water quality degradation:**Pollution in the Pra River has severely affected water treatment at water treatment plants, and in the Eastern Region, turbidity levels from mining were so high that water treatment plants had to be shut down temporarily.Tests commissioned by civil society indicate elevated concentrations of pollutants downstream from Asempa Gold. Polluted water cannot meet the "public health" criterion. Ghana Water must expend additional resources to treat compromised source water or risk service interruption to two district capitals.

3. **Environmental flow impacts:**The Volta River Basin Charter (Article 9) provides that the Basin's shared water resources shall be utilised to meet "domestic, socio-economic and environmental demands."Diverting a tributary and reducing Adom River flow threatens aquatic ecosystems, fisheries, and downstream livelihoods dependent on water quality and flow regime.

**Does this constitute "irreparable damage"?** 

The term "irreparable damage" means damage that cannot be undone or adequately remedied. Evidence of:
- Measurable loss of dry-season water availability to downstream users,
- Documented water quality degradation affecting public health,
- Alteration of tributary flow,

…establishes that further abstraction creates harm that cannot be reversed by Asempa Gold's unilateral action. The expansion does not restore lost flows to farmers or eliminate pollutants; it exacerbates the problem.

The standard is therefore triggered. The WRC must hold a public hearing and cannot issue a permit unless the applicant demonstrates that the expansion will not cause irreparable damage to water resources, public health, and the environment.

**Asempa Gold's Counter-Arguments and Their Legal Weight**

Asempa Gold makes three submissions:

1. **Mineral right as water entitlement:** "Its mining lease permits it to use water occurring within the area covered by its mineral right."

**Legal response:** This is expressly rejected by Act 703, section 17. A mineral right is a right to extract and process minerals; it does NOT automatically include a right to abstract water in any quantity.The statute requires separate "requisite approvals or licenses from the Water Resources Commission" before water use is lawful.The mineral right is a gateway; it does not bypass WRC approval.

2. **Environmental compliance:** "It has obtained the environmental approvals necessary for the expansion" and "maintains that its operations comply with all applicable environmental standards."

**Legal response:** Environmental approval by the EPA is a separate gate from WRC water-use approval.Prior to undertaking mineral operations, the holder must obtain permission from the Forestry Commission, an environmental permit from the EPA, and "where the proposed mineral operations is likely to use water in its natural state and/or affect water resources, the holder must also obtain a water right/use permit from the Water Resources Commission."[verbatim] EPA approval does not satisfy the WRC gate; it is a complementary but distinct requirement. The company's compliance with environmental standards does not address whether those standards are adequate to protect all downstream users or whether water availability itself is sufficient.

3. **Economic significance:** "The project is economically significant, employs more than 1,500 people and generates substantial mineral royalties and tax revenues."

**Legal response:** Economic significance is relevant to Tier 2 classification (socio-economic development use), but it does not override Tier 1 uses.Regulation 7 requires the WRC to be "guided by" domestic use as the primary criterion.The statute does not contain a "economic override" clause. As Ainuson argues,the mining industry can exist and continue to grow if the regulatory regime can strike a fair balance between the mining industry's effect on water use and the ability of the rest of the society to use water, and this conversation on striking a fair balance begins with the process of acquiring water rights.The company must bear the burden of demonstrating that its expansion can proceed without compromising domestic and public water supply uses.

**The District Assembly's Position and Legal Basis**

The District Assembly argues that "the expansion should not proceed until adequate water is guaranteed for communities."

This position aligns with the statutory framework.Under Article 10 of the Water Charter, where competing uses prevent all requirements from being met, "special attention shall be paid to the basic needs of human beings."Drinking water and domestic use for communities are basic human needs. Guaranteeing those needs takes legal precedence over mining expansion.

**Application of IWRM Principles**According to commentary, elements of IWRM include a holistic, integrated approach and main principles of public participation, the role of gender, and recognition of the economic value of water.In this case, IWRM requires the WRC to:
- **Holistically assess** all competing uses (mining, domestic, public supply, agriculture, environment) rather than treating the mining expansion in isolation.
- **Ensure public participation:**The WRC must hold a public hearing if the proposed use will have a negative impact on the natural resources of a basin.Affected farmers, communities, and Ghana Water must have a voice in the decision.
- **Recognize the economic value of water** not only to Asempa Gold but to the farmers, Ghana Water (serving two cities), and communities whose livelihoods and health depend on water.
- **Integrate agencies:**The enabling legislation ensures the WRC works with other agencies; the governing body of the WRC includes representatives from the EPA and Minerals Commission.The WRC cannot approve a permit in vacuum; it must coordinate with Minerals Commission (who granted the initial lease) and EPA (environmental compliance).

IWRM supports the conclusion that the expansion cannot proceed without demonstrating water sufficiency for all existing users.

**The Integrative Committee Process and Water Impact Assessment**The Minerals Commission's standing technical committee includes WRC representation. The WRC representative advises on water impacts. If the proposed operation will adversely affect water resources for which there can be no appreciable remedial action to reduce or minimize the adverse effect, the Minerals Commission may advise the Minister to set the land aside as ecologically fragile.In this case:
- Farmers report measurable loss of dry-season water since mining commenced.
- Water quality tests show pollution.
- The expansion will divert a tributary and increase abstraction.

These facts meet the threshold: adverse effects on water resources, with no "appreciable remedial action" by Asempa Gold to reduce them (Asempa Gold cannot undo the loss to farmers; it can only reduce its own operations). The WRC representative should advise the Minerals Commission to recommend that the Minister consider whether the affected area meets the "ecologically fragile" standard under section 4 of Act 703. This would bar the expansion.

Alternatively, if the Minerals Commission recommends proceeding, the WRC representative can condition any WRC water permit on:
- Demonstrable sufficiency of water for all Tier 1 uses (downstream communities, Ghana Water supply) at all seasons.
- Measurable water quality standards that meet Ghana Water's treatment requirements.
- Environmental flow protection for tributaries.
- Monitoring and compliance mechanisms.

**Statutory Hierarchy: Ranking the Competing Uses**

Apply Regulation 7 directly to the facts:

| Use | Tier | Status | Existing/Proposed | Priority Rank |
|-----|------|--------|-------------------|---------------|
| Downstream domestic (drinking, sanitation, household) | 1 (Primary) | Established | Existing | **1st** |
| Ghana Water public supply (two district capitals) | 1 (Primary) | Established | Existing | **1st** |
| Downstream irrigation (farmers) | 1 (Primary: domestic + basic agricultural needs) | Established | Existing | **1st** |
| Asempa Gold expansion (industrial mining) | 2 (Secondary: socio-economic development) | New gate | Proposed | **2nd** |
| Environmental flows (aquatic ecosystems) | 1 or 2 (Charter: "environmental demands"; Act 522 trust duty) | Established as ecosystem baseline | Ongoing | **1st–2nd** |

Where all Tier 1 uses cannot be met, Tier 2 (mining expansion) cannot proceed. The facts show:
- Dry-season water is already insufficient for all existing Tier 1 uses (farmers report loss; Ghana Water may face supply pressure).
- The expansion would exacerbate this insufficiency.

**Legal Conclusion on Priority:**

The expansion cannot satisfy Regulation 7's primary criterion (domestic use must be protected) without demonstrated water sufficiency. Since such sufficiency cannot be demonstrated on the facts, the statutory hierarchy mandates that the expansion be **refused** unless Asempa Gold can prove (1) no net loss to downstream communities or Ghana Water, (2) no irreparable harm to water quality or ecosystems, and (3) compliance with any water-emergency protocols under the Act.

---

## ConclusionGhanaian law establishes an explicit statutory hierarchy through Regulation 7 of the Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692): domestic water use is the primary guiding criterion; socio-economic development uses (including mining) are secondary; temporal priority favors first-in-time applications.The facts show that existing downstream users—communities drawing drinking and domestic water, Ghana Water supplying two district capitals, and farmers relying on seasonal irrigation—are Tier 1 uses established before or alongside Asempa Gold's initial mining operations. The proposed expansion is a Tier 2 use competing with these Tier 1 uses.The WRC's permit review standard requires that applications conform to national water policy and will not cause "irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment"; a public hearing is mandatory where the WRC considers the proposed use will have negative basin-wide impact.Evidence of dry-season water loss, documented pollution, and threatened tributary flow meets the "irreparable damage" threshold.The Water Charter for the Volta River Basin establishes that where competing uses prevent all requirements from being met, "special attention shall be paid to the basic needs of human beings."Drinking water and domestic supply for communities and cities are basic human needs that must take precedence.

Asempa Gold's mineral right does not entitle it to water independently;separate WRC approval is mandatory.Economic benefit to the company does not override statutory priority for domestic uses.

**The law does not permit the expansion to proceed on the facts as presented.** The WRC must refuse the permit unless Asempa Gold demonstrates (with independent verification) that the expansion will not reduce water availability to existing downstream users in any season, will not further degrade water quality, and will not cause irreparable environmental harm. The burden lies on the applicant, not on downstream users or the regulator.As Ainuson notes, the mining industry can exist and grow only if the regulatory regime strikes a fair balance between mining's effect on water and the rest of society's water use; this conversation begins with acquiring water rights.On these facts, fair balance requires the expansion to be **refused** unless conditions ensuring protection of all established Tier 1 uses can be met.

The proposed expansion is a Tier 2 use competing with these Tier 1 uses.The WRC's permit review standard requires that applications conform to national water policy and will not cause "irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment"; a public hearing is mandatory where the WRC considers the proposed use will have negative basin-wide impact. 【Water Implications of Large-Scale Land Acquisitions in Ghana — Williams, T.O.; Gyampoh, B.; Kizito, F. and Namara, R., Water Alternatives — p.11】Evidence of dry-season water loss, documented pollution, and threatened tributary flow meets the "irreparable damage" threshold.The Water Charter for the Volta River Basin establishes that where competing uses prevent all requirements from being met, "special attention shall be paid to the basic needs of human beings." 【Water Charter for the Volta River Basin — Final version, December 2018 — p.xxvii】Drinking water and domestic supply for communities and cities are basic human needs that must take precedence.

Asempa Gold's mineral right does not entitle it to water independently;separate WRC approval is mandatory. 【Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.36】Economic benefit to the company does not override statutory priority for domestic uses.

**The law does not permit the expansion to proceed on the facts as presented.** The WRC must refuse the permit unless Asempa Gold demonstrates (with independent verification) that the expansion will not reduce water availability to existing downstream users in any season, will not further degrade water quality, and will not cause irreparable environmental harm. The burden lies on the applicant, not on downstream users or the regulator.As Ainuson notes, the mining industry can exist and grow only if the regulatory regime strikes a fair balance between mining's effect on water and the rest of society's water use; this conversation begins with acquiring water rights. 【Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.25】On these facts, fair balance requires the expansion to be **refused** unless conditions ensuring protection of all established Tier 1 uses can be met.

# ISSUE 5: COMPETING DEMANDS FOR AVAILABLE WATER AND STATUTORY HIERARCHY

## Issue

How does Ghanaian law prioritize competing demands for water when a licensed mining operation seeks to expand its abstraction, and existing downstream users (domestic consumers, public water utilities, farmers, and environmental flows) rely on the same watercourse? Specifically: (a) does the law establish an explicit statutory hierarchy among mining, domestic consumption, public water supply, agriculture, and environmental requirements; (b) what criteria and legal standards must the Water Resources Commission apply when deciding whether to grant, refuse, or condition a water permit for the expansion; (c) whether existing downstream users and environmental flows have protected legal status; and (d) how Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) principles inform the allocation decision?

---

## Rule

**Primary Law: Statutory Hierarchy of Water Uses**

The Water Use Regulations, 2001 (L.I. 1692), Regulation 7 establishes that "In considering an application, the Commission shall be guided by (a) the prevailing water policy, (b) domestic water use, and (c) any other water use which fulfils the goals of national socio-economic development. Where the priorities of two applications are the same, the first in time shall be given the priority."

The hierarchy is explicit: **domestic water use is the primary guiding criterion**; socio-economic development uses (which may include mining and irrigation) are secondary; where two uses rank equally in tier, temporal priority (first application granted) determines allocation.

**Trust Duty and Public Interest**
"The property in and control of all water resources is vested in the President on behalf of, and in trust for the people of Ghana" (Water Resources Commission Act, 1996 (Act 522), section 12).

**No Standalone Mining Entitlement to Water**

The Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), section 17 provides that the holder of a mineral right must obtain "the requisite approvals or licenses from the Water Resources Commission before it may '…obtain, divert, impound, convey and use water from a river, stream, underground reservoir or watercourse within the land the subject of the mineral right'."

**Integration of Agencies: WRC Role in Mineral Permitting**

The standing technical committee of the Minerals Commission includes a representative from the Water Resources Commission. ## Application

**The Statutory Priority Framework and Asempa Gold's Expansion**

Start with Regulation 7 of L.I. 1692. It divides water uses into two tiers:
- **Tier 1 (Primary):** Domestic water use.
- **Tier 2 (Secondary):** Uses fulfilling national socio-economic development goals.

The Adom River serves multiple Tier 1 uses:
1. Drinking water for downstream communities.
2. Domestic activities (washing, sanitation) for residents.
3. Public water supply to two district capitals via Ghana Water Company Ltd (Ghana Water).

These are not new aspirations or future plans. They are **established existing uses** with settled beneficiaries.

Asempa Gold's proposed expansion is a Tier 2 use: industrial mining for economic development and foreign exchange. Mining generates royalties, tax revenue, and employment—classic socio-economic development goals.

**The Temporal Priority Rule and Its Application**

Regulation 7(2) provides that where two applications rank equally in priority tier, "the first in time shall be given the priority."

The facts establish that:
- Downstream communities have used the Adom River for drinking and domestic purposes presumably for decades, if not generations.
- Ghana Water has been abstracting from the river approximately 35 km downstream for an unspecified period to supply two district capitals.
- Asempa Gold's mining commenced at an unspecified date, and the expansion is now proposed.

On temporal grounds alone, the established domestic and public utility uses have priority over the expansion. The expansion is not the first application; it is an incremental increase to an already licensed operation, competing with pre-existing established uses.

**The "Irreparable Damage" Standard and the Evidence**

Regulation 4 of L.I. 1692 requires the WRC to refuse or condition permits that cause "irreparable damage to water resources, public health and the environment."

Three forms of harm are now documented:

1. **Reduction in dry-season flows:**
Mining operations have put stress on the quantity and quality of water in mining areas.

cites.title: Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.24
cites.quote:
As mineral operations have increased in
Ghana, it has put stress on the quantity and quality of water in mining areas2.

segments.text:
Farmers downstream report that "the volume of water available during the dry season has declined considerably since mining commenced." If the expansion proceeds, further reduction is predictable. This directly affects Tier 1 uses (domestic consumption by downstream communities and irrigators).

2. **Water quality degradation:**

Pollution in the Pra River has severely affected water treatment at water treatment plants, and in the Eastern Region, turbidity levels from mining were so high that water treatment plants had to be shut down temporarily.

cites.title: Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.25
cites.quote:
pollution in the Pra River had severely affected water treatment at the Daboase Water Treat‐
ment Plant which affects water supply to half of the consumers of the Ghana Water Compa‐
ny in the Western Region of Ghana4. In the Eastern Region of Ghana, the turbidity levels
were so high in river bodies as a result of mining activities that the Anyinam Water Treat‐
ment Plant, Bunso Water Treatment Plant and the Kyebi Water Treatment Plants had to be
shut down temporary5.

segments.text:
Tests commissioned by civil society indicate elevated concentrations of pollutants downstream from Asempa Gold. Polluted water cannot meet the "public health" criterion. Ghana Water must expend additional resources to treat compromised source water or risk service interruption to two district capitals.

3. **Environmental flow impacts:**
The Volta River Basin Charter (Article 9) provides that the Basin's shared water resources shall be utilised to meet "domestic, socio-economic and environmental demands."

cites.title: Water Charter for the Volta River Basin — Final version, December 2018 — p.xxvii
cites.quote:
In a coordinated and sustainable manner, the Basin’s shared water resources shall 
be utilised so that they meet the domestic, socio-economic and environmental 
demands.

segments.text:
Diverting a tributary and reducing Adom River flow threatens aquatic ecosystems, fisheries, and downstream livelihoods dependent on water quality and flow regime.

**Does this constitute "irreparable damage"?** 

The term "irreparable damage" means damage that cannot be undone or adequately remedied. Evidence of:
- Measurable loss of dry-season water availability to downstream users,
- Documented water quality degradation affecting public health,
- Alteration of tributary flow,

…establishes that further abstraction creates harm that cannot be reversed by Asempa Gold's unilateral action. The expansion does not restore lost flows to farmers or eliminate pollutants; it exacerbates the problem.

The standard is therefore triggered. The WRC must hold a public hearing and cannot issue a permit unless the applicant demonstrates that the expansion will not cause irreparable damage to water resources, public health, and the environment.

**Asempa Gold's Counter-Arguments and Their Legal Weight**

Asempa Gold makes three submissions:

1. **Mineral right as water entitlement:** "Its mining lease permits it to use water occurring within the area covered by its mineral right."

**Legal response:** This is expressly rejected by Act 703, section 17. A mineral right is a right to extract and process minerals; it does NOT automatically include a right to abstract water in any quantity.
The statute requires separate "requisite approvals or licenses from the Water Resources Commission" before water use is lawful.

cites.title: Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.36
cites.quote:
50 provides that the holder of a mineral right must obtain
the requisite approvals or licenses from the Water Resources Commission before it may “…
obtain, divert, impound, convey and use water from a river, stream, underground reservoir
or watercourse within the land the subject of the mineral right”51.

segments.text:
The mineral right is a gateway; it does not bypass WRC approval.

2. **Environmental compliance:** "It has obtained the environmental approvals necessary for the expansion" and "maintains that its operations comply with all applicable environmental standards."

**Legal response:** Environmental approval by the EPA is a separate gate from WRC water-use approval.

Prior to undertaking mineral operations, the holder must obtain permission from the Forestry Commission, an environmental permit from the EPA, and "where the proposed mineral operations is likely to use water in its natural state and/or affect water resources, the holder must also obtain a water right/use permit from the Water Resources Commission."

cites.title: Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.36
cites.quote:
Prior to undertaking mineral operations, the holder of mineral rights is also required
to obtain permission from the Forestry Commission47 as well as obtain an environmental
permit from the Environmental Protection Agency. Where the proposed mineral operations
is likely to use water in its natural state and/or affect water resources, the holder must also
obtain a water right/use permit from the Water Resources Commission.

segments.text:
[verbatim] EPA approval does not satisfy the WRC gate; it is a complementary but distinct requirement. The company's compliance with environmental standards does not address whether those standards are adequate to protect all downstream users or whether water availability itself is sufficient.

3. **Economic significance:** "The project is economically significant, employs more than 1,500 people and generates substantial mineral royalties and tax revenues."

**Legal response:** Economic significance is relevant to Tier 2 classification (socio-economic development use), but it does not override Tier 1 uses.
Regulation 7 requires the WRC to be "guided by" domestic use as the primary criterion.

The company must bear the burden of demonstrating that its expansion can proceed without compromising domestic and public water supply uses.

**The District Assembly's Position and Legal Basis**

The District Assembly argues that "the expansion should not proceed until adequate water is guaranteed for communities."

This position aligns with the statutory framework.
Under Article 10 of the Water Charter, where competing uses prevent all requirements from being met, "special attention shall be paid to the basic needs of human beings."

Drinking water and domestic use for communities are basic human needs. Guaranteeing those needs takes legal precedence over mining expansion.

**Application of IWRM Principles**
According to commentary, elements of IWRM include a holistic, integrated approach and main principles of public participation, the role of gender, and recognition of the economic value of water.

segments.text:
In this case, IWRM requires the WRC to:
- **Holistically assess** all competing uses (mining, domestic, public supply, agriculture, environment) rather than treating the mining expansion in isolation.
- **Ensure public participation:**
The WRC must hold a public hearing if the proposed use will have a negative impact on the natural resources of a basin.

Affected farmers, communities, and Ghana Water must have a voice in the decision.
- **Recognize the economic value of water** not only to Asempa Gold but to the farmers, Ghana Water (serving two cities), and communities whose livelihoods and health depend on water.

IWRM supports the conclusion that the expansion cannot proceed without demonstrating water sufficiency for all existing users.

**The Integrative Committee Process and Water Impact Assessment**

The Minerals Commission's standing technical committee includes WRC representation. The WRC representative advises on water impacts. If the proposed operation will adversely affect water resources for which there can be no appreciable remedial action to reduce or minimize the adverse effect, the Minerals Commission may advise the Minister to set the land aside as ecologically fragile.

mineral exploitation has as part of its members a representative from the Water Resources
Commission, Forestry Commission, Lands Commission, Geological Services Department

the Minerals Commission for processing, the Minerals Commission will take the views
of the representatives of the other agencies with respect to the technical competency of
the application as it affects their respective agency’s scope of work. In this direction, the
representative of the Water Resources Commission is able to advice the committee as to
the effect of the proposed mineral operations on water bodies in and around the mining
area. If the proposed mining operation will adversely affect water resources for which

Minerals Commission may advice the Minister to exercise his/her power under section 4
of the Minerals and Mining Act to set the land aside from mining for being an ecological
fragile area.

segments.text:
In this case:
- Farmers report measurable loss of dry-season water since mining commenced.
- Water quality tests show pollution.
- The expansion will divert a tributary and increase abstraction.

These facts meet the threshold: adverse effects on water resources, with no "appreciable remedial action" by Asempa Gold to reduce them (Asempa Gold cannot undo the loss to farmers; it can only reduce its own operations). The WRC representative should advise the Minerals Commission to recommend that the Minister consider whether the affected area meets the "ecologically fragile" standard under section 4 of Act 703. This would bar the expansion.

Alternatively, if the Minerals Commission recommends proceeding, the WRC representative can condition any WRC water permit on:
- Demonstrable sufficiency of water for all Tier 1 uses (downstream communities, Ghana Water supply) at all seasons.
- Measurable water quality standards that meet Ghana Water's treatment requirements.
- Environmental flow protection for tributaries.
- Monitoring and compliance mechanisms.

**Statutory Hierarchy: Ranking the Competing Uses**

Apply Regulation 7 directly to the facts:

| Use | Tier | Status | Existing/Proposed | Priority Rank |
|-----|------|--------|-------------------|---------------|
| Downstream domestic (drinking, sanitation, household) | 1 (Primary) | Established | Existing | **1st** |
| Ghana Water public supply (two district capitals) | 1 (Primary) | Established | Existing | **1st** |
| Downstream irrigation (farmers) | 1 (Primary: domestic + basic agricultural needs) | Established | Existing | **1st** |
| Asempa Gold expansion (industrial mining) | 2 (Secondary: socio-economic development) | New gate | Proposed | **2nd** |
| Environmental flows (aquatic ecosystems) | 1 or 2 (Charter: "environmental demands"; Act 522 trust duty) | Established as ecosystem baseline | Ongoing | **1st–2nd** |

Where all Tier 1 uses cannot be met, Tier 2 (mining expansion) cannot proceed. The facts show:
- Dry-season water is already insufficient for all existing Tier 1 uses (farmers report loss; Ghana Water may face supply pressure).
- The expansion would exacerbate this insufficiency.

**Legal Conclusion on Priority:**

The expansion cannot satisfy Regulation 7's primary criterion (domestic use must be protected) without demonstrated water sufficiency. Since such sufficiency cannot be demonstrated on the facts, the statutory hierarchy mandates that the expansion be **refused** unless Asempa Gold can prove (1) no net loss to downstream communities or Ghana Water, (2) no irreparable harm to water quality or ecosystems, and (3) compliance with any water-emergency protocols under the Act.

---

segments.text: On these facts, fair balance requires the expansion to be **refused** unless conditions ensuring protection of all established Tier 1 uses can be met.

sources.title: Acquiring Water Rights in Mineral Operations in Ghana — Kweku Ainuson — p.39
sources.quote:
The standing committee in recognition of the symbiotic nature of
mineral exploitation has as part of its members a representative from the Water Resources
Commission, Forestry Commission, Lands Commission, Geological Services Department
and the Environmental Protection Agency. Therefore, when an application is submitted to
the Minerals Commission for processing, the Minerals Commission will take the views
of the representatives of the other agencies with respect to the technical competency of
the application as it affects their respective agency’s scope of work. In this direction, the
representative of the Water Resources Commission is able to advice the committee as to
the effect of the proposed mineral operations on water bodies in and around the mining
area. If the proposed mining operation will adversely affect water resources for which
there can be no appreciable remedial action to reduce or minimize the adverse effect, the
Minerals Commission may advice the Minister to exercise his/her power under section 4
of the Minerals and Mining Act to set the land aside from mining for being an ecological
fragile area. In the same vein, if by the nature of the application the applicant must obtain
a water use license the Water Resources Commission can indicate such requirement so that
the grant of the mineral right by the Minister will be subject to a water use license obtained
from the Water Resources Commission.
